title: Portfolio Setup Instructions
text:
Welcome to MUSA 5080! This guide will help you set up your personal portfolio repository for the semester.


By the end of this setup, you’ll have: - Your own portfolio repository on GitHub - live website showcasing your work - A place to document your learning journey




This is what you are building: Dr. Delmelle’s sample portfolio




Before starting, make sure you have: - [ ] A GitHub account (create one here if needed) - [ ] Quarto installed on your computer (download here) - [ ] R and RStudio installed





You should already be in your personal repository (created when you accepted the GitHub Classroom assignment). Now let’s personalize it!



Click on the _quarto.yml file
Click the pencil icon (✏️) to edit
Change "Your Name - MUSA 5080 Portfolio" to include your actual name
Example: "Jane Smith - MUSA 5080 Portfolio"
Click “Commit changes” at the bottom





Click on the index.qmd file
Click the pencil icon (✏️) to edit
Update the “About Me” section with your information:

Your name and background
Your email address
Your GitHub username
Why you’re taking this course

Click “Commit changes”





Navigate to the weekly-notes folder
Click on week-01-notes.qmd
Click the pencil icon (✏️) to edit
Fill in your notes from the first class
Click “Commit changes”





This step makes your portfolio visible as a live website!

Go to Settings: Click the “Settings” tab at the top of your repository
Find Pages: Scroll down and click “Pages” in the left sidebar
Configure Source:

Source: Select “Deploy from a branch”
Branch: Select “main”
Folder: Select “/ docs”

Save: Click “Save”
Wait: GitHub will show a message that your site is being built (this takes 1-5 minutes)





Find Your URL: After a few minutes, GitHub will show your website URL at the top of the Pages settings

It will look like: https://yourusername.github.io/repository-name

Visit Your Site: Click the link to see your live portfolio!
Bookmark It: Save this URL - you’ll submit it to Canvas





Copy your live website URL
Go to the Canvas assignment
Submit your URL





If you want to work on your computer and see changes before publishing:


# Replace [your-repo-url] with your actual repository URL
git clone [your-repo-url]
cd [your-repository-name]



# Edit your files using RStudio
# Preview your changes:
quarto render
quarto preview

# When ready, save your changes:
git add .
git commit -m "Update portfolio"
git push
Your live website will automatically update when you push changes!




Each week you’ll: 1. Create a new file: weekly-notes/week-XX-notes.qmd 2. Copy the template from week-01-notes.qmd 3. Fill in your reflections and key concepts 4. Commit and push your changes






Wait longer: GitHub Pages can take up to 10 minutes to build
Check Actions tab: Look for any red X marks indicating build failures
Verify Pages settings: Make sure you selected “main” branch and “/docs” folder





Check permissions: Make sure you’re in YOUR repository, not the template
Sign in: Ensure you’re signed into GitHub





Check YAML syntax: Make sure your _quarto.yml file has proper formatting
Verify file names: Files should end in .qmd not .md
Look at error messages: The Actions tab will show specific error details





Don’t panic! Every change is tracked in Git
See history: Click the “History” button on any file to see previous versions
Revert changes: You can always go back to a previous version






Commit often: Save your work frequently with descriptive commit messages
Use branches: For major changes, create a new branch and merge when ready
Preview locally: Use quarto preview to see changes before publishing
Keep it professional: This portfolio can be shared with future employers!
Document everything: Good documentation is as important as good analysis

Outside Class: - Office Hours: Mondays 1:30-3:00 PM - Email: delmelle@design.upenn.edu - GitHub Issues: Create an issue in your repository for technical problems - Canvas Discussion: Post questions others might have too

title: Week 3 Notes - Data Visualization & Exploratory Analysis
text:
Part 3: Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)
•   Mindset: Detective work—explore distributions, patterns, anomalies, reliability.
•   Workflow: Load & inspect → Assess reliability (MOE, CV) → Visualize → Explore relationships → Identify anomalies → Document limitations.
•   Distributions: Look for skewness, outliers, multimodality.
•   Data quality via visualization: Small populations often show higher uncertainty—risk of systematic undercounting.
•   Best practices (Jurjevich et al., 2018):
•   Always report MOEs or note omission.
•   Use CV thresholds: <12% reliable, 12–40% somewhat reliable, >40% unreliable.
•   Reduce uncertainty by aggregating data.
•   Test statistical significance for comparisons.
•   Policy focus: Check for geographic concentration, demographic disparities, temporal changes, and reliability of estimates.

title: Spatial Predictive Analysis: Predicting Burglaries Using Sanitation Complaints
text:
This analysis applies spatial predictive modeling techniques to predict burglaries in Chicago using sanitation code complaints as the primary predictor variable. Following the “broken windows theory,” we hypothesize that areas with more sanitation violations may also experience higher burglary rates due to lower social cohesion and reduced guardianship.


By completing this analysis, I will demonstrate the ability to:

Create a fishnet grid to aggregate point-level crime and 311 data
Calculate spatial features from 311 complaint data
Diagnose spatial autocorrelation using Local Moran’s I
Fit and interpret Poisson and Negative Binomial regression for count data
Implement spatial cross-validation (Leave-One-Group-Out)
Compare model predictions to a Kernel Density Estimation baseline
Evaluate model performance using appropriate metrics

title: Spatial Predictive Analysis: Predicting Burglaries Using Sanitation Complaints
text:
1.1 Load Chicago Spatial Boundaries
In this step, I load the administrative boundaries of Chicago. These boundaries are essential for spatial analysis as they provide the geographic reference framework. I use the Illinois State Plane coordinate system (ESRI:102271), which minimizes distortion in the Chicago area and uses feet as the unit of measurement.


Code
# Load police districts (used for spatial cross-validation)
policeDistricts <- 
  st_read("https://data.cityofchicago.org/api/geospatial/24zt-jpfn?method=export&format=GeoJSON") %>%
  st_transform('ESRI:102271') %>%
  dplyr::select(District = dist_num)

# Load police beats
policeBeats <- 
  st_read("https://data.cityofchicago.org/api/geospatial/n9it-hstw?method=export&format=GeoJSON") %>%
  st_transform('ESRI:102271') %>%
  dplyr::select(Beat = beat_num)

# Load Chicago boundary
chicagoBoundary <- 
  st_read("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/urbanSpatial/Public-Policy-Analytics-Landing/master/DATA/Chapter5/chicagoBoundary.geojson") %>%
  st_transform('ESRI:102271')


Why ESRI:102271 Coordinate Reference System?
This coordinate system is particularly appropriate for Chicago because it minimizes spatial distortion in this region, uses feet as units, and allows for accurate distance calculations.

title: Spatial Predictive Analysis: Predicting Burglaries Using Sanitation Complaints
text:
1.2 Load 2017 Burglary Data
In this step, I load the 2017 burglary data. These are the crimes we want to predict using sanitation complaint features.


Code
# Load burglaries from local shapefile
burglaries_2017 <- st_read("data/burglaries.shp") %>%
  st_transform('ESRI:102271')


Data Provenance Matters
These data are recorded by the Chicago Police Department. It’s important to note that these data may have biases:

Unreported burglaries (victims didn’t call police)
Incidents police chose not to record
Downgraded offenses
Spatial bias (more patrol = more recorded crime)

title: Spatial Predictive Analysis: Predicting Burglaries Using Sanitation Complaints
text:
1.3 Visualize Burglary Point Data
In this step, I create two visualizations: a point map showing the location of each burglary, and a density plot showing the spatial concentration of burglaries.


Code
# Point map
p1 <- ggplot() + 
  geom_sf(data = chicagoBoundary, fill = "gray95", color = "gray60") +
  geom_sf(data = burglaries_2017, color = "#d62828", size = 0.1, alpha = 0.4) +
  labs(
    title = "Burglary Locations",
    subtitle = paste0("Chicago 2017, n = ", nrow(burglaries_2017))
  ) +
  theme_void()

# Density surface
p2 <- ggplot() + 
  geom_sf(data = chicagoBoundary, fill = "gray95", color = "gray60") +
  stat_density_2d_filled(
    data = data.frame(st_coordinates(burglaries_2017)),
    aes(X, Y),
    alpha = 0.7,
    bins = 8
  ) +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(
    option = "plasma",
    direction = -1,
    guide = "none"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Density Surface",
    subtitle = "Kernel density estimation"
  ) +
  theme_void()

# Combine plots
p1 + p2 + 
  plot_annotation(
    title = "Spatial Distribution of Burglaries in Chicago"
  )









Observed Spatial Patterns
The visualizations reveal that burglaries are not uniformly distributed across Chicago. I observe that burglaries are concentrated in two areas of the city. These patterns may reflect differences in socioeconomic conditions, building types, or policing practices.

title: Spatial Predictive Analysis: Predicting Burglaries Using Sanitation Complaints
text:
2.1 Understanding the Fishnet
A fishnet grid is a tool for converting irregular point data into regular grid cells. This allows us to:

Aggregate count data
Calculate spatial features
Apply regression models

I use a 500m × 500m grid, which provides a good balance between capturing spatial variation and maintaining sufficient sample sizes.


Code
# Create 500m x 500m grid
fishnet <- st_make_grid(
  chicagoBoundary,
  cellsize = 500,  # 500 meters per cell
  square = TRUE
) %>%
  st_sf() %>%
  mutate(uniqueID = row_number())

# Keep only cells that intersect Chicago
fishnet <- fishnet[chicagoBoundary, ]


Why Use a Regular Grid?
Using a regular grid rather than existing boundaries has several advantages: consistent cell sizes, avoids the Modifiable Areal Unit Problem (MAUP), and is independent of administrative boundaries. However, the disadvantage is that it may not align with meaningful social or economic boundaries.

title: Spatial Predictive Analysis: Predicting Burglaries Using Sanitation Complaints
text:
2.2 Aggregate Burglaries to Grid
In this step, I count the number of burglaries in each grid cell. This converts point data into count data that can be used for regression modeling.


Code
# Spatial join
burglaries_fishnet <- st_join(burglaries_2017, fishnet, join = st_within) %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  group_by(uniqueID) %>%
  summarize(countBurglaries = n())

# Join back to fishnet
fishnet <- fishnet %>%
  left_join(burglaries_fishnet, by = "uniqueID") %>%
  mutate(countBurglaries = replace_na(countBurglaries, 0))

title: Spatial Predictive Analysis: Predicting Burglaries Using Sanitation Complaints
text:
2.3 Visualize Aggregated Counts


Code
# Visualize aggregated counts
ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = fishnet, aes(fill = countBurglaries), color = NA) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(
    name = "Burglaries",
    option = "plasma",
    trans = "sqrt"  # Square root transformation for better visualization
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Burglaries per Grid Cell",
    subtitle = "500m × 500m grid, 2017"
  ) +
  theme_void()









Count Distribution
Most grid cells have relatively few burglaries, but certain areas have significantly higher burglary counts. Using a square root transformation helps visualize this right-skewed distribution. The high percentage of zero-count cells suggests overdispersion.

title: Spatial Predictive Analysis: Predicting Burglaries Using Sanitation Complaints
text:
3.1 Why Use Sanitation Complaints?
Following “broken windows theory,” sanitation code violations are signs of neighborhood disorder. Areas with more sanitation complaints may also experience higher burglary rates due to:

Lower social cohesion
Less community surveillance (“eyes on the street”)
Perception of neglect
Reduced informal guardianship

We’ll use sanitation complaints as a predictor for burglaries, similar to how the class example used abandoned vehicles.

title: Spatial Predictive Analysis: Predicting Burglaries Using Sanitation Complaints
text:
3.2 Load 2017 Sanitation Complaints


Code
# Load 2017 sanitation complaints from local CSV file
sanitation_2017 <- read_csv(
  "data/311_Service_Requests_-_Sanitation_Code_Complaints_-_Historical_20251115.csv", 
  show_col_types = FALSE
) %>%
  # Parse date and filter for 2017
  mutate(date = mdy(`Creation Date`)) %>%
  filter(year(date) == 2017) %>%
  # Remove records without coordinates
  filter(!is.na(Latitude) & !is.na(Longitude)) %>%
  # Convert to spatial object
  st_as_sf(coords = c("Longitude", "Latitude"), crs = 4326) %>%
  st_transform('ESRI:102271') %>%
  mutate(date = as.Date(date))


Critical Question About Data
These 311 complaints are reported by residents. Consider potential biases: Different neighborhoods may have different reporting rates, Digital divide may affect access to 311 system, Gentrifying areas may have higher complaint rates. Complaints reflect reporting behavior, not just actual conditions

title: Spatial Predictive Analysis: Predicting Burglaries Using Sanitation Complaints
section: 3.3 Visualize Relationship Between Sanitation and Burglaries
text:
3.3 Visualize Relationship Between Sanitation and Burglaries


Code
# Aggregate sanitation complaints to fishnet
sanitation_fishnet <- st_join(sanitation_2017, fishnet, join = st_within) %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  group_by(uniqueID) %>%
  summarize(countSanitation = n())

# Join to fishnet
fishnet <- fishnet %>%
  left_join(sanitation_fishnet, by = "uniqueID") %>%
  mutate(countSanitation = replace_na(countSanitation, 0))

# Side-by-side comparison
p1 <- ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = fishnet, aes(fill = countSanitation), color = NA) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(
    name = "Count",
    option = "magma",
    trans = "sqrt"
  ) +
  labs(title = "Sanitation Complaints") +
  theme_void()

p2 <- ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = fishnet, aes(fill = countBurglaries), color = NA) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(
    name = "Count",
    option = "plasma",
    trans = "sqrt"
  ) +
  labs(title = "Burglaries") +
  theme_void()

p1 + p2 +
  plot_annotation(
    title = "Are sanitation complaints and burglaries spatially correlated?"
  )









Visual Assessment
By comparing these two maps, we can see areas with high sanitation complaints also tend to have high burglary rates. Visual correlation provides initial evidence for our modeling approach, though we’ll need regression to quantify the relationship while controlling for spatial effects.

title: Spatial Predictive Analysis: Predicting Burglaries Using Sanitation Complaints
text:
3.4 Calculate Sanitation Complaint Features
Following the class example structure, we create three spatial features from sanitation complaints:


Code
# Feature 1: Count of sanitation complaints per cell (already calculated)
# Feature 2: Mean distance to nearest 3 sanitation complaints
# Handle cases where there are fewer complaints or infinite distances
fishnet_coords <- st_coordinates(st_centroid(fishnet))
sanitation_coords <- st_coordinates(sanitation_2017)

if(nrow(sanitation_coords) >= 3) {
  nn_result <- get.knnx(sanitation_coords, fishnet_coords, k = 3)
  
  fishnet <- fishnet %>%
    mutate(
      sanitation.nn = rowMeans(nn_result$nn.dist),
      # Replace any infinite values with max finite value
      sanitation.nn = ifelse(is.infinite(sanitation.nn), 
                            max(sanitation.nn[is.finite(sanitation.nn)], na.rm = TRUE), 
                            sanitation.nn),
      # Scale to reasonable range (divide by 1000 to get in thousands of feet)
      sanitation.nn = sanitation.nn / 1000
    )
} else {
  fishnet <- fishnet %>%
    mutate(sanitation.nn = 0)
}

# Feature 3: Distance to sanitation complaint hot spots
# First, identify hot spots using Local Moran's I
coords_mat <- as.matrix(fishnet_coords)
neighbors <- knn2nb(knearneigh(coords_mat, k = 5))
weights <- nb2listw(neighbors, style = "W", zero.policy = TRUE)

local_moran_sanitation <- localmoran(fishnet$countSanitation, weights)

fishnet <- fishnet %>%
  mutate(
    sanitation_moran_i = local_moran_sanitation[, 1],
    sanitation_moran_p = local_moran_sanitation[, 5],
    sanitation_moran_sig = sanitation_moran_p < 0.05,
    sanitation_cluster = case_when(
      !sanitation_moran_sig ~ "Not Significant",
      countSanitation >= mean(countSanitation) & sanitation_moran_i > 0 ~ "High-High",
      countSanitation < mean(countSanitation) & sanitation_moran_i > 0 ~ "Low-Low",
      countSanitation >= mean(countSanitation) & sanitation_moran_i < 0 ~ "High-Low",
      countSanitation < mean(countSanitation) & sanitation_moran_i < 0 ~ "Low-High"
    )
  )

# Identify hot spots
sanitation_hotspots <- fishnet %>%
  filter(sanitation_cluster == "High-High")

# Calculate distance to nearest hot spot
if(nrow(sanitation_hotspots) > 0) {
  fishnet <- fishnet %>%
    mutate(
      dist_to_sanitation_hotspot = as.numeric(st_distance(geometry, st_union(sanitation_hotspots))),
      # Scale to thousands of feet
      dist_to_sanitation_hotspot = dist_to_sanitation_hotspot / 1000
    )
} else {
  fishnet <- fishnet %>%
    mutate(dist_to_sanitation_hotspot = 0)
}


Three Features Explained

Count: Direct measure of sanitation problems in the cell
Nearest Neighbor Distance: Local context - are you near sanitation issues? (scaled to thousands of feet)
Distance to Hot Spots: Proximity to concentrated disorder areas (scaled to thousands of feet)

Note: We scale distances to thousands of feet to improve numerical stability in regression models.

title: Spatial Predictive Analysis: Predicting Burglaries Using Sanitation Complaints
text:
3.5 Visualize Sanitation Hot Spots


Code
ggplot() +

text:
6.1 Why Spatial Cross-Validation?
Standard cross-validation randomly splits data. But with spatial data, this means training on cells right next to test cells (information leakage!). Leave-One-Group-Out (LOGO) cross-validation trains on all districts except one, then tests on the held-out district. This provides a more realistic assessment of how the model performs in new areas.


Code
# Get unique districts
districts <- unique(fishnet_model$District)
cv_results <- tibble()

for (i in seq_along(districts)) {
  
  test_district <- districts[i]
  
  # Split data
  train_data <- fishnet_model %>% filter(District != test_district)
  test_data <- fishnet_model %>% filter(District == test_district)
  
  # Fit model on training data - three-feature model
  model_cv <- glm.nb(
    countBurglaries ~ countSanitation + log(sanitation.nn + 0.1) + 
      log(dist_to_sanitation_hotspot + 1),
    data = train_data
  )
  
  # Predict on test data
  test_data <- test_data %>%
    mutate(
      prediction = predict(model_cv, test_data, type = "response")
    )
  
  # Calculate metrics
  mae <- mean(abs(test_data$countBurglaries - test_data$prediction))
  rmse <- sqrt(mean((test_data$countBurglaries - test_data$prediction)^2))
  
  # Store results
  cv_results <- bind_rows(
    cv_results,
    tibble(
      Fold = i,
      Test_District = test_district,
      N_Test = nrow(test_data),
      MAE = mae,
      RMSE = rmse
    )
  )
}

title: Spatial Predictive Analysis: Predicting Burglaries Using Sanitation Complaints
text:
Model Limitations

Data Bias: Both crime data and 311 complaints reflect reporting behavior, not just actual conditions. Areas with more active community engagement may have higher report rates.
Overdispersion: The data shows significant overdispersion, which is why the Negative Binomial model is more appropriate than Poisson.
Zero Inflation: Approximately 31.8% of grid cells have no burglaries, which may warrant a zero-inflated model.
Spatial Autocorrelation: Although we used spatial features, spatial autocorrelation may still exist in the residuals.
Temporal Assumption: This model assumes the relationship between sanitation and burglaries is stable over time, which may not hold.
Scale Sensitivity: We scaled distance variables to improve model convergence, which affects coefficient interpretation.

title: Spatial Predictive Analysis: Predicting Burglaries Using Sanitation Complaints
text:
Policy Implications
When using such predictive models for resource allocation or intervention decisions, it’s essential to recognize:

Reporting Bias: Systematic differences in reporting rates may exist across communities
Causal vs. Correlation: Association between sanitation and burglaries doesn’t prove causation
Potential for Feedback Loops: Increased enforcement in predicted areas may generate more reports
Equity Concerns: Models based on historical data may perpetuate existing inequalities

title: Space-Time Prediction of Bike Share Demand: Philadelphia Indego - Q2 2024
text:
Operational Implications
With an MAE of 0.74 trips per station-hour—roughly 112.1% of average demand—the model works well enough for most routine operations. The problem is that routine operations aren’t where rebalancing failures hurt most. A two-trip error at 30th Street Station during morning rush leaves commuters stranded. Special events create demand spikes the model never sees coming. Nice summer weekends produce exactly the kind of unpredictable recreational demand that breaks our lag-based predictions.
Full automation may be a mistake. The model handles typical weekday patterns reliably, which covers most hours at most stations. Deploy it there. For high-demand stations during peak periods, for known events, for unusual weather—keep operators in the decision loop. Build in safety margins at critical locations rather than optimizing to the prediction. The 80/20 split makes sense: let the model handle routine rebalancing, reserve human judgment for high-stakes decisions.

title: Space-Time Prediction of Bike Share Demand: Philadelphia Indego - Q2 2024
text:
Equity Considerations
The demographic patterns are more concerning than they first appear. Higher-income neighborhoods show larger prediction errors, while areas with high transit ridership show smaller errors. This likely reflects behavioral differences: transit-dependent neighborhoods have rigid, predictable commute patterns, while car-owning areas use bikes more opportunistically. The model handles routine commutes well but struggles with discretionary trips.
The equity problem isn’t bias in the technical sense—the model isn’t systematically under-serving certain neighborhoods. The problem is operational feedback loops. When predictions fail in lower-income areas with limited alternatives, residents stop trusting the system. Rebalancing staff naturally prioritize areas where predictions work well. Service quality diverges, usage patterns diverge further, and the system becomes less equitable over time without anyone explicitly choosing that outcome.

title: Space-Time Prediction of Bike Share Demand: Philadelphia Indego - Q2 2024
text:
Model Limitations
Several important patterns sit outside what this model can capture. Special events generate demand spikes with no predictive signal in historical data. University calendars matter—Penn and Drexel exam periods shift demand substantially—but we’re not tracking them. Construction projects reroute trips in ways lag features can’t anticipate. Infrastructure changes like new bike lanes take weeks to show up in ridership patterns.
The core assumption that past predicts future breaks down as cities change. New construction shifts residential patterns. Businesses close or open. Commute routes evolve. We’re also using current weather when people actually make decisions based on forecasts. The independence assumption is clearly wrong—when one station empties, demand doesn’t just disappear, it shifts to nearby stations or people choose different modes entirely. These network effects matter but our station-by-station approach now can’t see them.

title: Space-Time Prediction of Bike Share Demand: Philadelphia Indego - Q2 2024
text:
Seasonal Differences
Q2 2024 shows 30-40% higher ridership than Q1 2025, driven primarily by temperature. Spring and summer riders are selective—demand peaks between 60-75°F and drops off sharply outside that range. Winter ridership concentrates among commuters willing to ride in any weather, producing more stable but lower baseline demand. Weekend patterns shift accordingly: Q2 sees substantial recreational demand, Q1 stays commute-focused throughout the week. Model performance differs less than the underlying patterns would suggest. MAE in Q2 runs around 0.74 versus 0.65-0.75 in Q1 (estimated). Weather features carry more weight in Q2 models, lag features dominate in Q1.

Part 1: Healthcare Access for Vulnerable Populations

Research Question
Which Pennsylvania counties have the highest proportion of vulnerable populations (elderly + low-income) living far from hospitals?
Your analysis should identify counties that should be priorities for healthcare investment and policy intervention.


Required Analysis Steps
Complete the following analysis, documenting each step with code and brief explanations:

Step 1: Data Collection (5 points)
Load the required spatial data: - Pennsylvania county boundaries - Pennsylvania hospitals (from lecture data) - Pennsylvania census tracts
Your Task:

# Load required packages

Step 2: Get Demographic Data

# Get demographic data from ACS
pa_demo <- get_acs(
  geography = "tract",
  state = "PA",
  variables = c(

    median_income = "B19013_001",       
    pop_65_74 = "B01001_020",

# Pivot the data to wide format
pa_demo_wide <- pa_demo %>%
  select(GEOID, NAME, variable, estimate) %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = variable, values_from = estimate,
    values_fill = 0
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    pop_65p = rowSums(across(c(pop_65_74, pop_75_84, pop_85p)), na.rm = TRUE),
    elderly_pct = 100 * pop_65p / total_pop

# Join to tract boundaries

Step 3: Define Vulnerable Populations
Identify census tracts with vulnerable populations based on TWO criteria: 1. Low median household income (choose an appropriate threshold) 2. Significant elderly population (choose an appropriate threshold)
Your Task:

# Filter for vulnerable tracts based on your criteria
# Define thresholds
income_threshold <- 50000   
elderly_threshold <- 10    

# Identify vulnerable tracts
vulnerable_tracts <- tracts_with_demo %>%
  filter(!is.na(median_income)) %>%
  mutate(
    low_income = median_income < income_threshold,
    sign_elderly = elderly_pct > elderly_threshold,
    vulnerable = low_income | sign_elderly
  )

# Summaries
summary_vals <- list(
  pa_median = median(tracts_with_demo$median_income, na.rm = TRUE),
  n_vul = sum(vulnerable_tracts$vulnerable),
  pct_vul = round(mean(vulnerable_tracts$vulnerable) * 100, 1),
  n_low = sum(vulnerable_tracts$low_income),

What elderly population threshold did you choose and why? Elderly population threshold chosen: 10%. Tracts where more than 10% of residents are aged 65 or older were considered to have a significant elderly population, a common demographic baseline in vulnerability analyses.

Step 4: Calculate Distance to Hospitals
For each vulnerable tract, calculate the distance to the nearest hospital.
Your Task:

# Transform to appropriate projected CRS
# EPSG 2272 is optimized for southern Pennsylvania counties such as Philadelphia, Lancaster, Chester, and York
target_crs <- 2272

# Reproject all layers
pa_counties_p <- st_transform(pa_counties, target_crs)
hospitals_p   <- st_transform(hospitals,   target_crs)
vul_p         <- st_transform(vulnerable_tracts, target_crs)

# Calculate distance from each tract centroid to nearest hospital
# tract centroids
vul_centroids <- st_centroid(vul_p)

# nearest hospital index
nn_idx <- st_nearest_feature(vul_centroids, hospitals_p)

# distance in feet -> miles
dists_ft <- st_distance(vul_centroids, hospitals_p[nn_idx, ], by_element = TRUE)
dists_mi <- units::set_units(dists_ft, "mi") |> units::drop_units()

# attach results
vulnerable_tracts_dist <- vul_p |>
  mutate(
    nearest_hosp_idx = as.integer(nn_idx),
    dist_to_hosp_mi  = dists_mi
  )

# join hospital name if a name field exists
name_field <- intersect(c("NAME","Name","name","HOSP_NAME","HOSPITAL","HospName"), names(hospitals_p))[1]
if (!is.na(name_field)) {
  vulnerable_tracts_dist <- vulnerable_tracts_dist |>
    mutate(nearest_hosp_name = hospitals_p[[name_field]][nearest_hosp_idx])
}

# summary statistics
avg_dist <- mean(vulnerable_tracts_dist$dist_to_hosp_mi, na.rm = TRUE)
min_dist <- min(vulnerable_tracts_dist$dist_to_hosp_mi, na.rm = TRUE)
max_dist <- max(vulnerable_tracts_dist$dist_to_hosp_mi, na.rm = TRUE)
n_over15 <- sum(vulnerable_tracts_dist$dist_to_hosp_mi > 15, na.rm = TRUE)

cat(
  "Average distance to nearest hospital:", round(avg_dist, 2), "miles\n",
  "Minimum distance:", round(min_dist, 2), "miles\n",
  "Maximum distance:", round(max_dist, 2), "miles\n",
  "Number of tracts more than 15 miles from nearest hospital:", n_over15, "\n"
)

What is the maximum distance? 32.84 miles
How many vulnerable tracts are more than 15 miles from the nearest hospital? 127




Step 5: Identify Underserved Areas
Define “underserved” as vulnerable tracts that are more than 15 miles from the nearest hospital.
Your Task:

# Create underserved variable
# Definition: vulnerable tracts with distance > 15 miles

vulnerable_tracts_dist <- vulnerable_tracts_dist %>%
  mutate(underserved = dist_to_hosp_mi > 15)

# Counts and percentages
n_underserved  <- sum(vulnerable_tracts_dist$underserved, na.rm = TRUE)
n_with_dist    <- sum(!is.na(vulnerable_tracts_dist$dist_to_hosp_mi))
n_vulnerable   <- nrow(vulnerable_tracts_dist)
pct_underserved <- round(100 * n_underserved / n_with_dist, 1)

cat(
  "Underserved tracts:", n_underserved, "\n",
  "Percent underserved (of tracts with a distance):", pct_underserved, "%\n",
  "Vulnerable tracts total:", n_vulnerable, "\n",
  "With valid distance:", n_with_dist, "\n"
)

Does this surprise you? Why or why not? Yes, a bit less than I expected. ————————————————————————



Step 6: Aggregate to County Level
Use spatial joins and aggregation to calculate county-level statistics about vulnerable populations and hospital access.
Your Task:

# find county name field in pa_counties_p

  c("NAME","NAME20","NAMELSAD","COUNTY","COUNTY_NAM","COUNTYNAME","County","county","NAME10"),
  names(pa_counties_p)

Do areas in Philadelphia with higher concentrations of children have adequate spatial access to schools within a 0.5-mile walking distance?

Conduct spatial analysis

Use at least TWO spatial operations to answer your research question.
Required operations (choose 2+): - Buffers - Spatial joins - Spatial filtering with predicates - Distance calculations - Intersections or unions - Point-in-polygon aggregation
Your Task:

# Your spatial analysis
# Build 0.5-mile service buffer of schools
school_buf <- schools %>%
  st_buffer(buf_ft) %>%      # service area
  st_union() %>%             # dissolve overlaps
  st_as_sf()

# Tract-level coverage and areal-weighted children counts
area_total   <- st_area(acs_children)
overlap_idx  <- st_intersects(acs_children, school_buf)
has_overlap  <- lengths(overlap_idx) > 0
area_covered <- units::set_units(0, "ft^2")
area_covered[has_overlap] <- st_area(st_intersection(acs_children[has_overlap, ], school_buf))

tracts_cov <- acs_children %>%
  mutate(
    area_total   = area_total,
    area_covered = area_covered,
    pct_covered  = pmin(1, as.numeric(area_covered / area_total)),
    children_in_service = child_pop * pct_covered,

title: Week 5 Notes - Introduction to Linear Regression
text:
Week 5 Summary — Introduction to Linear Regression

Statistical Learning Basics • Goal: find relationships between predictors (X) and an outcome (Y). • Two main objectives: • Prediction — making accurate forecasts. • Inference — understanding which variables matter and how. • Methods: • Parametric assumes a specific relationship form (e.g., linear regression). • Non-parametric makes fewer assumptions but needs more data.
Linear Regression Concepts • Assumes a linear relationship between variables. • Uses Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) to estimate coefficients. • Advantages: simple, interpretable, widely used. • Limitations: assumes linearity, sensitive to outliers, depends on model assumptions.
Prediction vs Inference ￼ • Inference: focuses on explaining relationships and coefficient meaning. • Prediction: focuses on accuracy and practical forecasting. • A statistically strong model can still be ethically biased.
Model Evaluation • In-sample fit uses R²; shows how much variation the model explains. • Out-of-sample performance uses train/test split or cross-validation. • Overfitting occurs when a model fits training data too closely but predicts poorly. • RMSE and MAE measure prediction error.
Regression Assumptions • Linearity: residuals should be random around zero. • Constant variance: avoid heteroskedasticity (test with Breusch–Pagan). • Normal residuals: important for inference, less for prediction. • No multicollinearity: predictors shouldn’t be highly correlated (check VIF). • No influential outliers: check leverage and Cook’s distance.
Improving Models • Add meaningful predictors to improve fit. • Use log transformations for curved relationships. • Include categorical variables when appropriate. • Balance model complexity with interpretability.
Key Ideas • R² alone doesn’t prove a model is good; always test predictions. • Diagnostic checks ensure assumptions hold. • Visualization and interpretation are as important as computation. • Ethical reflection matters in applying models to real data.

title: Week 4 Notes - Spatial Data & GIS Operations in R
text:
1. Importance of Spatial Analysis
•   Moves beyond tabular demographic data by asking where patterns occur.
•   Supports real policy questions: locating underserved areas, understanding spatial clustering, comparing jurisdictions, and identifying environmental justice concerns.
•   Spatial bias in algorithms can reinforce inequality; spatial understanding helps design fairer systems.

title: Week 4 Notes - Spatial Data & GIS Operations in R
text:
2. Spatial Data Fundamentals
•   Vector model: points (locations), lines (networks), polygons (areas) with geometry + attributes.
•   sf package: integrates spatial data with tidyverse; treats spatial objects as data frames with geometry columns.
•   Common formats: Shapefiles, GeoJSON, KML/KMZ, PostGIS connections.

title: Week 4 Notes - Spatial Data & GIS Operations in R
text:
3. Spatial Operations
•   Subsetting: st_filter() + predicates (st_intersects, st_touches, st_within). Predicate choice determines spatial relationship logic.
•   Spatial joins: merge datasets based on spatial relationships.
•   Distance/Area calculations: require attention to coordinate reference systems (CRS).
•   Dot (.) acts as placeholder in pipes for the data being transformed.

title: Week 4 Notes - Spatial Data & GIS Operations in R
text:
4. Geometry Operations
•   Buffers: create zones around features for accessibility or impact analysis. Buffer size can vary by attribute.
•   Intersection vs. Filter:
•   st_filter() selects entire features based on relation.
•   st_intersection() clips geometries for overlay analysis.
•   Union: merges multiple geometries.
•   Spatial aggregation: summarizes attributes across spatial boundaries.

title: Week 4 Notes - Spatial Data & GIS Operations in R
text:
5. Coordinate Reference Systems (CRS)
•   Projection matters because the Earth is curved but maps are flat.
•   GCS (e.g., WGS84 EPSG:4326): lat/long, good for global/web, not for measurement.
•   PCS (e.g., State Plane, UTM, Albers): planar coordinates, good for area/distance calculations.
•   Use st_crs() to check, st_set_crs() if missing, and st_transform() to change CRS for analysis.
•   Transform when measuring, buffering, or working locally.

title: Week 4 Notes - Spatial Data & GIS Operations in R
text:
6. Policy Analysis Workflow
Typical spatial workflow: 1. Load spatial and attribute data. 2. Check and transform CRS. 3. Join datasets. 4. Apply spatial operations (buffers, intersections, distance). 5. Aggregate results. 6. Visualize with maps/charts. 7. Interpret for policy.
Example: Healthcare access analysis • Project data to local CRS. • Create 25 km buffers around hospitals. • For each county: check if intersecting buffer and calculate distance to nearest hospital. • Join results with demographics for further analysis.

title: Week 6 Notes - Spatial Machine Learning & Advanced Regression
text:
Summary of Week 6 Lecture: Spatial Machine Learning & Advanced Regression ￼
⸻

Baseline Model Building • Began with a simple linear regression predicting SalePrice from LivingArea (structural feature only). • Coefficient: each extra sq ft adds ≈ $216. • R² ≈ 0.13 → explains only 13% of variation. • Missing factors: location, amenities, neighborhood quality, crime, schools.

⸻

Adding Predictors • Adding number of bathrooms increased R² slightly (to 0.14). • Demonstrated diminishing returns from structural-only models. • Emphasized the need for spatial variables to capture “location, location, location.”

⸻

Introducing Spatial Data • Converted tabular data to spatial (sf) format using coordinates. • Transformed CRS from EPSG:4326 to MA State Plane for accurate distance measures. • Joined parcels with neighborhood polygons using st_join(). • Visualized median prices by neighborhood, showing clear spatial clustering: • Back Bay, Beacon Hill, South End highest. • Dorchester, Roxbury, Mattapan lowest.

⸻

Regression with Categorical (Dummy) Variables • Used neighborhood name (name) as a factor. • R automatically creates dummy variables for each neighborhood. • One neighborhood (Allston) becomes the reference category. • Model interpretation: • Positive coefficient → more expensive than Allston. • Negative coefficient → cheaper than Allston. • Example: identical houses differ by millions between Back Bay ($8.5M) and Roxbury ($0.33M).

⸻

Interaction Effects • Question: does square footage matter equally in all areas? • Built interaction models: • Model 1 (no interaction): same slope everywhere. • Model 2 (interaction): slope differs by neighborhood wealth. • Defined “wealthy neighborhoods” = Back Bay, Beacon Hill, South End, Bay Village. • Result: • Wealthy areas have much steeper slopes (≈ $985/sq ft vs. $95 in others). • Confirms Luxury Premium Hypothesis — larger homes in wealthy areas command disproportionate premiums.

⸻

Conceptual Takeaways • Spatial features and fixed effects are critical to avoid biased estimates. • Spatial autocorrelation violates OLS independence assumptions. • Remedies: include location terms, fixed effects, or spatial regression models. • Understanding geography improves both predictive accuracy and policy relevance in housing analytics.

⸻
Key Terms: baseline model, dummy variable, fixed effects, interaction term, spatial join, CRS transformation, hedonic model, Tobler’s First Law, spatial autocorrelation.
